pumac-2024-number-theory-b-03.title: Only residues mod 3 matter
pumac-2024-number-theory-b-03.body:
If $f(x)\equiv r\pmod3$ for some positive integer $x$, then every $n\equiv r\pmod 3$ with $n>f(x)$ is $f(x)+3y$ for $y= rac{n-f(x)}3\ge1$. So $f$ is full iff $f(x)$ takes all three residues mod $3$ as $x$ varies (if a residue class is missed, infinitely many integers are not representable).

The residue of $f(x)$ depends on $x mod3$, so we need $f(0),f(1),f(2)$ distinct mod $3$: $C,\ A+B+C,\ A+2B+C\pmod3$. This is equivalent to $B
ot\equiv0$, $A+B
ot\equiv0$, $A+2B
ot\equiv0\pmod3$. If $B\equiv1$ this means $A
ot\equiv2,\ A
ot\equiv1$; if $B\equiv2$, $A
ot\equiv1,\ A
ot\equiv2$. In both cases $A\equiv0\pmod 3$.

Count: $A\in\{3,6,9\}$ ($3$ ways), $B\in\{1,\dots,9\}$ not a multiple of $3$ ($6$ ways), $C$ any ($9$ ways): $3\cdot6\cdot9=162$.

**Answer: 162**

pumac-2024-number-theory-b-04.title: Discriminant a perfect square
pumac-2024-number-theory-b-04.body:
Rational roots need $B^2-4\cdot196\cdot135=B^2-105840=k^2$, so $(B-k)(B+k)=105840=2^4\cdot3^3\cdot5\cdot7^2$ with $B>0$. Both factors have the same parity, hence are even: $B-k=2u$, $B+k=2v$, $uv=26460=2^2\cdot3^3\cdot5\cdot7^2$ and $B=u+v$.

We need $B$ coprime to $2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$. $B$ odd means exactly one of $u,v$ is even; the even one then contains all of $2^2$. Let the odd one be $d$ and the other $4e$, with $de=3^3\cdot5\cdot7^2=6615$ and $B=d+4e$. For $B$ to be coprime to $3,5,7$, no prime of $3,5,7$ may divide both $d$ and $e$, so each full prime power $27,5,49$ goes entirely to $d$ or to $e$: $8$ choices.

| $d$ | $e$ | $B=d+4e$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6615 | 26461 |
| 5 | 1323 | 5297 |
| 27 | 245 | 1007 |
| 49 | 135 | 589 |
| 135 | 49 | 331 |
| 245 | 27 | 353 |
| 1323 | 5 | 1343 |
| 6615 | 1 | 6619 |

All eight are coprime to $196\cdot135$, and their sum is $26461+5297+1007+589+331+353+1343+6619=42000$.

**Answer: 42000**

pumac-2024-number-theory-b-05.title: Linear permutations
pumac-2024-number-theory-b-05.body:
Taking $b=1$ repeatedly gives $\sigma(n)\equiv n\,t\pmod{100}$ with $t=\sigma(1)$. For $\sigma$ to be a permutation of $\{1,\dots,100\}$ (values read mod $100$ with $0\leftrightarrow100$), $t$ must be a unit mod $100$ ($40$ choices), and each such $t$ works.

So $f(s)$ is the sum of the distinct residues of $s\,t\bmod100$ (taking $0$ as $100$) over units $t$.
- For $s$ coprime to $100$, $st$ runs over all $40$ units: $f(s)=$ the sum of units in $[1,100]$ $=40\cdot50=2000$ (this is the maximum).
- For $s=50$: $50t\equiv50\pmod{100}$ for odd $t$, so $f(50)=50$ (the minimum). One can check no $s$ gives less (for $s=100$ the value is always $100$).

Difference: $2000-50=1950$.

**Answer: 1950**

pumac-2024-number-theory-b-06.title: Count by the prime gcd
pumac-2024-number-theory-b-06.body:
The $a\le m$ with $\gcd(a,m)=p$ correspond to $a=pa'$ with $\gcd(a',m/p)=1$, so $r(m)=\sum_{p\mid m}\varphi(m/p)$. Also $\varphi(m/p)=\frac{\varphi(m)}p$ if $p^2\mid m$ and $\frac{\varphi(m)}{p-1}$ if $p\,\|\,m$. So $r(m)=\varphi(m)$ iff
$$\sum_{p\mid m}t_p=1,\qquad t_p=\frac1p\ (p^2\mid m)\ \text{ or }\ \frac1{p-1}\ (p\,\|\,m).$$
- $p=2$ contributes $1$ (if $2\,\|\,m$) or $\frac12$; $p=3$: $\frac12$ or $\frac13$; $p=5$: $\frac14$ or $\frac15$; $p=7$: $\frac16$ or $\frac17$; ...
- If $2\,\|\,m$ then $m=2$ (any other prime would push the sum above $1$).
- Otherwise $4\mid m$ with $\frac12$ from $p=2$, and the rest must sum to $\frac12$: either $3\,\|\,m$ alone ($m=3\cdot2^a$, $a\ge2$: $12,24,48,96,192$), or $9\mid m$ ($\frac13$) together with $7\,\|\,m$ ($\frac16$): $m=4\cdot9\cdot7=252$; other combinations (e.g. $5$, $11$, $13$,...) would need $m\ge300$.

So the solutions are $2,12,24,48,96,192,252$ with sum $626$. (The degenerate $m=1$ has $r(1)=0$ and no $a<1$ coprime to $1$ under the literal wording; with the standard $\varphi(1)=1$ it is not a solution, so it is excluded.)

**Answer: 626**

pumac-2024-number-theory-b-07.title: Reduce to abundant odd numbers
pumac-2024-number-theory-b-07.body:
Let $n=2m$ with $m$ odd. The even divisors of $n$ are $2d$ for $d\mid m$; the even proper divisors are $2d$ with $d\mid m$, $d\ne m$, so their sum is $2(\sigma(m)-m)$. The odd divisors of $n$ are exactly the divisors of $m$, all proper, with sum $\sigma(m)$.

$n$ is nice iff $2\sigma(m)-2m>\sigma(m)$, i.e. $\sigma(m)>2m$: $m$ is an odd abundant number. The smallest odd abundant number is $945=3^3\cdot5\cdot7$ ($\sigma=1920>1890$). Hence the smallest nice $n\equiv2\pmod4$ is $2\cdot945=1890$.

**Answer: 1890**

pumac-2024-number-theory-b-08.title: Kummer's theorem
pumac-2024-number-theory-b-08.body:
By Kummer, $v_2\binom ni$ equals the number of carries when adding $i$ and $n-i$ in binary. We count cells with at least $2$ carries.

Total cells in rows $1$ to $63$: $\sum_{n=1}^{63}(n+1)=2079$.
- Cells with $0$ carries (odd entries): $2^{s(n)}$ in row $n$, where $s(n)$ is the number of $1$'s in the binary form of $n$. Since $\sum_{n=0}^{63}2^{s(n)}=3^6=729$, rows $1$ to $63$ give $728$.
- Cells with exactly $1$ carry ($v_2=1$): in row $n$ there are (number of occurrences of the block "10" in the binary form of $n$)$\cdot2^{s(n)-1}$. Over $6$-bit strings: each of the $5$ adjacent bit positions holds "10", and the other four bits are free: $\sum2^{s-1}=\sum_t\binom4t2^t=81$. Total $5\cdot81=405$.

Red cells: $2079-728-405=946$.

**Answer: 946**

pumac-2024-number-theory-b-08.title: Direct count
pumac-2024-number-theory-b-08.body:
Computing $\binom ni\bmod4$ directly for all $1\le n\le63$ and $0\le i\le n$ and counting zeros also gives $946$.

**Answer: 946**
